_metadata.title: India Climatic Zones — BEE ECBC / IMD Classification
standards: Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) — Energy Conservation Building Code (ECBC) 2017
IMD Climatological Atlas of India — Climate Zone Demarcation
National Building Code (NBC) 2016 — Part 8, Section 1: Climate and Site
GRIHA Manual v2015 — Climate Responsive Design Parameters
_metadata.note: Zone boundaries follow BEE ECBC 2017 district-wise demarcation. City-to-zone mapping is based on ECBC Table 2 and NBC 2016 Appendix E. Thermal parameters are based on IMD 30-year climate normals (1991-2020).

Composite.description: Hot summers, cold winters, and a well-defined monsoon season. Temperature range is extreme across the year (>15°C diurnal swing in summer). Moderate humidity during monsoon; dry and cold in winter. Dominant in North Indian plains — Punjab, Haryana, Delhi NCR, western UP, and parts of Rajasthan.
Composite.wind_prevailing_direction: NW in winter, SW in monsoon
passive_design_strategies: Heavy thermal mass walls (230mm brick or equivalent) for temperature damping
Deep shading overhangs on south and west facades — projection factor ≥ 0.5
Cross-ventilation with operable windows on north and south elevations
Courtyard typology to create shaded microclimate
Evaporative cooling supplementation viable in dry season
Insulated roof (U-value ≤ 0.4 W/m²K per ECBC) — critical for summer comfort
Light-coloured roof surface or green roof for solar reflectance
Double-glazed windows with external shading on south/west
Night ventilation cooling strategy (flush hot air in evening)
Composite.key_bioclimatic_challenge: Managing extreme summer heat (>42°C) while accommodating cold winter nights (<5°C) and high monsoon humidity
material_recommendations: Fly ash brick / AAC blocks (low thermal conductivity)
Lime plaster (breathable, hygroscopic — manages humidity)
Terracotta roof tiles with air gap
Timber louvres for shading

Hot & Dry.description: Very hot dry summers (>40°C), mild winters, and negligible rainfall (<400mm annually). Extremely low humidity year-round. Dominant in Rajasthan, Kutch, and parts of Karnataka/Andhra Deccan plateau. Diurnal temperature swing can be >20°C — useful for night cooling strategies.
Hot & Dry.wind_prevailing_direction: SW hot dry winds (loo) in summer
passive_design_strategies: Compact courtyard form to minimise exposed surface area
Very thick walls (350–450mm) for maximum thermal mass
Flat earth roofs with insulation for thermal damping
Wind towers (baoli) and evaporative cooling towers
Minimal window area on south/west — max 20% WWR
Screens and jaali (lattice) for filtered daylighting without heat gain
Underground/semi-basement spaces for natural cooling
Xeriscaping — drought-resistant native vegetation
Hot & Dry.key_bioclimatic_challenge: Extreme solar radiation and heat gain reduction while maximising night cooling potential
material_recommendations: Rammed earth / compressed stabilised earth blocks (CSEB)
Adobe / mud plaster
White/reflective surface finishes
Stone (sandstone, granite) for high thermal mass

Warm & Humid.description: High temperatures (32–38°C) combined with persistently high humidity (70–90% RH) year-round. Very heavy monsoon rainfall. Dominant along coastal India — Kerala, coastal Karnataka, Goa, coastal Tamil Nadu, Odisha, West Bengal, and coastal Maharashtra (Konkan). The combination of heat and humidity makes this the most thermally challenging zone for human comfort.
Warm & Humid.wind_prevailing_direction: SW (monsoon) — very strong, NE in winter
passive_design_strategies: Maximise natural cross-ventilation — elongated east-west building orientation
Elevated ground floor on stilts (traditional) for airflow below building
Deep veranda and overhanging eaves (min 1.2m projection) for rain and sun protection
Louvred shutters and jali screens — maximise airflow with rain protection
Open-plan interiors to facilitate air movement
Roof ventilation ridge vents and wind scoops
Avoid heavy thermal mass — lightweight construction responds faster to ventilation
Permeable landscape to manage high runoff and maintain microclimate humidity balance
Warm & Humid.key_bioclimatic_challenge: Continuous humidity management and air movement facilitation — thermal mass is counter-productive
material_recommendations: Laterite stone (local, breathable)
Bamboo and engineered timber (lightweight, renewable)
Clay/terracotta roof tiles with steep pitch
Lime-based renders (breathable, anti-fungal)

Temperate.description: Mild summers (20–30°C), cold winters (-5°C to 10°C), heavy snowfall above 1500m elevation. Moderate rainfall (800–1500mm). Dominant in HP, Uttarakhand hills, J&K foothills, and Sikkim/NE hill states. Two distinct seasons — pleasant summer and harsh winter. Cold nights even in summer months.
passive_design_strategies: South-facing orientation to maximise winter solar gain
Insulated walls and roof — critical for winter heating (U-value ≤ 0.35 W/m²K)
Double/triple glazed windows on south; minimal openings on north
Trombe wall or sunspace for passive solar heating
Compact building form to reduce heat loss surface area
Snow-proof roof design (steep pitch ≥ 40° or structural snow load calculation)
Protected entryway/airlock vestibule to prevent cold air infiltration
Earth-sheltering on north side for insulation
Temperate.key_bioclimatic_challenge: Winter heating load dominates — passive solar and insulation critical
material_recommendations: Deodar/pine timber (local, excellent insulator)
Stone masonry (local — slate, granite) with internal insulation
Mud/rammed earth with external insulation cladding
Double-walled construction with insulation fill

Cold.description: Very cold winters (-20°C to -30°C), short cool summers (10–20°C), heavy snowfall (2–6m annual snow accumulation above 3000m). Dominant in Ladakh, upper Himachal (Lahaul-Spiti, Kinnaur), Arunachal highland zones, and Uttarakhand high altitude regions. Extreme wind-chill factor. Very short growing/construction season.
Cold.wind_prevailing_direction: Strong katabatic mountain winds, NW winter blizzards
passive_design_strategies: Maximum insulation in all building elements — multi-layer wall assembly
Small compact building footprint — minimise surface-to-volume ratio
Sunspace/conservatory on south for solar gain buffer
Airtight construction with controlled mechanical ventilation (HRV/ERV)
Double/triple glazed south-facing windows — thermopane mandatory
Earth-bermed north wall for insulation and wind protection
Rammed earth or stone thermal mass to store solar gain
Snow-load structural design mandatory (IS 875 Part 4)
Cold.key_bioclimatic_challenge: Extreme cold survivability — heating and insulation are life-safety concerns, not just comfort
material_recommendations: Rammed earth (traditional — excellent insulator and thermal mass)
Compressed earth blocks with mud plaster
Timber (pine/poplar — local, renewable insulator)
EPS/XPS rigid foam insulation for modern construction

amritsar_detailed_profile.climate_summary: Amritsar experiences a continental climate with extreme summer heat (April–June reaching 42–46°C), a defined south-west monsoon (July–September, ~650mm annual rainfall), and cold winters (December–January with minimum temperatures of 2–6°C and occasional frost). The city lies in the Punjab plains at 234m AMSL on the Indo-Gangetic alluvial tract.
design_implications: Critical summer shading required — overhangs and courtyard design
Night ventilation viable in pre-monsoon season (low humidity, high diurnal swing)
Winter heating load not insignificant — insulated walls beneficial
Monsoon drainage planning essential — July peak rainfall
Green roof/cool roof viable for thermal load reduction
